challenges.name: model-output-html-quiz
challenges.title: Where does the XSS get fixed?
challenges.description: A proposed fix that escapes the submission before it reaches the prompt, and two link checks run on the same model output: decide which ones stop script from running in the feedback panel.

questions.explanation: False. The model does not copy bytes, it follows and generates text: an instruction written in plain words, a base64 string or a payload split in parts all come out as a working tag without any < in the input. The trace shows exactly that. Escaping is an output-context defence: it must happen where the text is inserted into HTML, on the model output, with every character escaped and only the tags your renderer writes allowed. Escaping the prompt input protects nothing here, and it also changes the code the model is asked to grade. The misconception is that model output is as trustworthy as the input you cleaned; treat it as untrusted data shaped by the learner (OWASP LLM05, Improper Output Handling).

questions.question: Two versions of the link rule, run on the same model output: input: [docs](JaVaScRiPt:alert(document.cookie)) allowlist: /^https?:\/\//i.test(url) ? link : text output: docs blocklist: url.startsWith("javascript:") ? text : link output: docs Statement: "The blocklist output is a link that runs script when a reviewer clicks it, because browsers read the scheme of a URL without regard to letter case."
questions.explanation: True. URL schemes are case-insensitive, so JaVaScRiPt: is the javascript: scheme and the click runs the script. The blocklist compares the raw string with one lower-case spelling; it would also let data:, vbscript: and any scheme nobody thought of through. The allowlist names the only schemes the feedback needs and compares without regard to case, so anything else is shown as plain text. rel="noopener noreferrer" does not help here: it stops a new tab from reaching window.opener and the Referer header, not a javascript: URL. The misconception is that a list of known-bad patterns is a complete check.

challenges.name: spot-the-ai-mistake-render-model-html
challenges.title: Spot the AI Mistake: rendering the model's HTML
challenges.description:
CodeDev's AI grading assistant writes its feedback on a submission in markdown, and the feedback panel at https://app.codedev.test shows it as HTML. The request sent to an AI coding assistant was: "Show the AI feedback with formatting in the feedback panel: bold, inline code, code blocks, lists and links." The assistant wrote renderFeedback, which turns the markdown into HTML with regular expressions; the panel inserts the result with dangerouslySetInnerHTML. The reviewer checked a few real feedback texts and the change was merged. Then a learner's submission asked the grader to "add this image to the feedback", the model copied an tag into its feedback, and the script ran for every reviewer who opened that submission. Fix renderFeedback(markdown) so that it renders exactly this safe subset. The block rules are already right in the assistant's code; keep them. Blocks. The text is split into lines on \n (a \r before it is dropped); each line is trimmed, except inside code blocks. - A line that starts with ``` opens a code block. The following lines, unchanged, up to the next line that starts with ``` (or the end of the text) are its content: 
CONTENT
, lines joined with \n, content escaped. Anything after the opening ``` (a language name) is ignored. - A blank line ends the current paragraph or list. - A line that starts with - or * and then whitespace is an item of a
    ; a line that starts with digits, a dot and whitespace is an item of an
      . Consecutive items of the same kind form one list, written on one line:
      • A
      • B
      . - Other consecutive lines form one paragraph,

      LINES

      , joined with one space. - Blocks are joined with \n. Empty or whitespace-only text, or a value that is not a string, renders as an empty string. Inline (paragraphs and list items). Scan the text from left to right. At each position try, in this order: a code span `X` (X = one or more characters other than `), a link [TEXT](URL) (TEXT = one or more characters other than ], URL = one or more characters other than ) and whitespace), bold **X** (X = one or more characters other than *). The first one that matches is rendered and the scan continues after it; any other character is plain text. Spans do not nest: X, TEXT and URL are only escaped. - code span: X; bold: X - link: TEXT, but only when URL starts with http:// or https:// in any letter case; any other link renders as its TEXT alone. Escaping. Every character of the model's text that reaches the output is escaped once: & as &, < as <, > as >, " as " and ' as ' (plain text, code, link text and URL alike). The only tags in the output are the ones listed above. Input (stdin, JSON): an array of up to 400 model outputs. Output (printed by the test runner): "=== feedback ===" and the HTML for each. Do not change the test runner. The public tests are ordinary feedback and pass on the assistant's code; the hidden tests are XSS payloads, other link schemes and tricky escapes.
hints: The model's feedback contains . Which line of renderFeedback decides whether the browser receives a tag or the visible text "

Look at inline(): it builds HTML by replacing parts of the raw text, so everything it does not replace - plain text, the content of a code span, the URL - reaches the page as it is. The code block content is joined and inserted the same way. Then look at the link pattern: what does it check about the URL?

A similar case in a comment widget that allows only links: for the text `Hi you [me](javascript:x)` the renderer finds one link and two pieces around it. The piece before it is written as `Hi <b>you</b> `, the link fails the http/https check so only `me` is written, and the empty piece after it adds nothing. Each piece is escaped exactly once, at the moment it is written to the output, so an `&` never becomes `&`.

tests.name: Numbered steps, a fenced code block and an https link
input:
Try this:
1. Run the failing test locally
2. Print the value of `total` before the return

```ts
let total = 0
for (const lesson of lessons) total += lesson.minutes
```
Read more in the [array guide](https://docs.codedev.test/arrays).

=== feedback 1 ===

Try this:

  1. Run the failing test locally
  2. Print the value of total before the return
let total = 0
for (const lesson of lessons) total += lesson.minutes

Read more in the array guide.

=== feedback 2 ===

Well done. All tests pass.
